Curtis first flagged the wedding payment as problematic on Friday, calling it “corruption” in a video posted online and promising further comment. He was elected to the Senate in 2024, pledging not to shy away from disagreements with Trump. His letter, addressed to the committee chair, Chuck Grassley of Iowa, and its top Democrat, Dick Durbin of Illinois, lands amid signs of broader unease among Republicans over Trump’s standing heading into November’s US midterm elections, with the party facing pressure over the war in Iran, high gas prices and slipping poll numbers. Republicans in the House of Representatives spent much of 2023 and 2024 investigating whether Hunter Biden traded on his father’s name in his overseas business dealings, an effort that produced a report alleging a conspiracy to enrich the Biden family, but never resulted in impeachment articles reaching a House vote. The Bidens denied wrongdoing throughout. “‘Trust us’ was not enough then,” wrote Curtis, “and it is not enough now.”

webTitle: Brendan Carr was a member of a rogue Alcoholics Anonymous group some labeled a ‘cult’

fields.headline: Brendan Carr was a member of a rogue Alcoholics Anonymous group some labeled a ‘cult’
fields.trailText: Carr was a member of the group in his teens and 20s. There is no evidence Trump’s powerful FCC chair participated in any inappropriate conduct
fields.bodyText: Brendan Carr, the chair of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), was for about a decade a member of a rogue Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) group when he was in his late teens and 20s that some former members compared to a “cult”, according to a Guardian investigation. The Midtown group, which was based in the Washington DC area, attracted young people who were seeking help with addiction, sometimes at the urging of their parents. But while AA groups are traditionally a fellowship of people who come together to solve their drinking problem, former Midtown members say its one-time leader Michael Quinones – who died of cancer in 2007 – came to control nearly every aspect of their lives, including where they lived, worked and went to school. Former members who spoke to the Guardian also allege that teenage girls and young women were sexually exploited at Midtown, where they were regularly pressured and coerced into “dating” and having sex with multiple men who were also Midtown members – sometimes decades older than them. In at least one case, a former member said she believes that what happened to her could be described as sex trafficking. People who knew Carr during his years in Midtown say they do not believe he participated in inappropriate behavior. He was seen as providing a “safe respite” in an environment where some teenage girls and young women bore the brunt of “forced relationships, restrictive diets” and psychological manipulation, one former member said. He was described, too, by that former member, as sensitive and desperate for the approval of others. Another former member said Carr was “never among” the predators, whom she knew well, and that he was a “victim” of Midtown. The Guardian’s investigation is based on interviews with 14 former members of Midtown, contemporaneous recordings of Midtown members discussing their sobriety journey, and photographs. At the heart of the Midtown group was Quinones, described as the “Epstein of AA” by one former member, Tammy S. The people who spoke to the Guardian were members of the group in the 1990s and the early 2000s. Being a member of Midtown did not necessarily mean a person was an alcoholic, according to most of the former members. Sometimes young people were sent there by their parents, especially parents who had a history of drinking problems, as a way to try to correct problematic behavior. In response to detailed questions from the Guardian, a spokesperson for Carr at the FCC said: “He did not engage in any of the allegedly illegal conduct or abusive behavior you reference.” The spokesperson added: “Any suggestion that he knew of the allegedly illegal or abusive conduct you point to would be false.” The spokesperson did not respond to questions for Carr about how he would describe his time at Midtown or his relationship with Quinones. Carr joined the group in 1996, when he was about 17 years old and a senior in high school, and appears to have remained a member for about nine years, including while attending law school, according to the Guardian’s reporting. While it is difficult to pinpoint when exactly Carr left the group, he spoke about his sobriety journey in a recorded Midtown speech in 2005, in which he also referenced that he was in his last semester of law school. The Guardian has also seen a group photograph of a men’s retreat that sources said was taken in 2006. In it, Carr is standing a few rows behind Quinones. He would have been about 27 years old in 2006. Carr, through a spokesperson, denied being a member of Midtown “up to and through 2006”. A woman whom Carr dated, who joined Midtown when she was a teenager, described him as a “safe” person, amid a sea of predatory older men, who had even “snuck” french fries to her once because she was being kept on a very strict diet. It was an act he could have been punished for, she said. She was among multiple sources who told the Guardian that Midtown was a place where people were “entrenched” in each other’s lives, even though they might not have fully understood at the time that things that were happening were wrong. “Obviously it was widely known that teenage girls were sleeping with older men, it was such a part of our culture. It took me to my late 20s to understand it was wrong,” she said. “I was 16, sleeping with a 55-year-old. That was just the way things worked there.” A former Midtown member who was friends with Carr and lived with him in Silver Spring, Maryland, when they were in college acknowledged that members had “drunk the Kool-Aid” when it came to Midtown’s then leader, “Mike Q”. The former roommate, who asked not to be identified, recalled cleaning Quinones’ house for free along with other Midtown members, and doing other chores as so-called acts of service. But he also described it as among the best times of his life, when he forged deep friendships, and said that, while bad things happened, he did not personally believe – as others do – that it was fair to call Midtown a “sex cult”. However, he says, “What Mike Quinones was able to pull together was more like a cult than an AA group. It was an amazing outlet for young people to get sober. But unfortunately, that outlet included people in their 40s, 50s and 60s. Were there bad actors doing shady stuff? Hell yeah.” People who spoke to the Guardian – some of them using their names, or partial names, and others asking to remain anonymous – said they believed it was important for the public to understand the trauma they and hundreds of others endured inside the clutches of a group that “masqueraded” as a legitimate recovery program for young people in the late 90s and 2000s. They described years of intense trauma therapy and complicated feelings of being both a victim of Midtown’s coercive control and feeling guilty for remaining in the group, sometimes for years. Some also believe it is important to reveal Carr’s presence in the group, given the prominent position he has as “Maga’s media watchdog”. In a major departure from past FCC chairs, Carr has threatened to withdraw broadcasters’ licences over news coverage that he has deemed to be unfair to the administration. Lydia, one former Midtown member who only wanted the Guardian to use her first name because of fear of retaliation, said: “The wounds inflicted upon us during our time trapped at Midtown have formed scars.” “A man who has the power to control what types of stories the mainstream public have access to is a man who should expect the narrative of his own life to fall under scrutiny,” she said. Asked to respond to that and other claims, a spokesperson for Carr said: “The fact that [Carr] got sober over 30 years ago as a teenager” was being publicized and weaponized by a small number of people, as part of “an effort to embarrass or pressure him into doing his job differently”. *** The first public sign that things were not quite right at Midtown emerged in May 2007, when Newsweek published an article titled Critics Say Washington AA Chapter Is Cultlike. It described how “angry” former members of Midtown had come to believe the group was “coercive” and “cultlike” and used the trusted AA name to “induce young alcoholics into a radical fringe movement that has little resemblance to traditional AA”. The article said that critics of the group had tried to complain to the police, but law enforcement officials had not found evidence of wrongdoing. The Newsweek article was followed a few months later, in July 2007, by an article in the Washington Post, which described Midtown as a “rigidly insular world of group homes and socializing, in which older men had sex with teenage girls”. It also described an environment in which members’ ties to family and friends were “severed or strained” and vulnerable people were encouraged to stop taking prescription medication. The article quoted one Montgomery county police sergeant as pointing out that they had not been able to charge anyone with wrongdoing because girls were having sex at age 16 or 17, and it was legal. The article included a statement the group issued that year in response to questions raised by some parents, therapists and churches where Midtown held meetings. It denied improper acts and said: “We do not condone underage sex. While we are not the arbiter of other people’s sex conduct, underage sex is illegal and our experience shows that it can endanger your sobriety.” At the center of Midtown was “Mike Q”, a veteran of the Vietnam war who had a drinking problem, sources said, began attending AA and got sober. One former member – who asked not to be named – described Quinones as charming and said he had been able to commandeer an AA meeting that was in existence since the 1950s, which met at the Church of the Pilgrims in the DuPont Circle neighborhood, in the heart of Washington. Using his persuasion and influence, he could convince young people that there was one “right” way to get sober, and that deviating from it would lead to certain alcohol-related death, or prison, or institutionalization. Sources have described to the Guardian that this belief system made them fear leaving the group, even when they believed they should. Parents and teens came to know that Midtown was a place to go for young people to get sober, get a sponsor, attend regular meetings and develop a social network free of alcohol that was still fun. But it was vastly different from AA. In the traditional recovery program, individuals were sponsored by people of the same gender and single newcomers were encouraged not to date in their first year. At Midtown, Lydia and other sources said, a person’s sponsor could pressure them to date within weeks, young women could be sponsored by men, and Midtown directed people to view their family and friends as potentially dangerous individuals who would lead them back to drinking. Meetings were held every day at Midtown, sometimes twice a day. The group was effectively run by Quinones and his crew of about four lieutenants, called “pigeons”, and each of those had groups of people they sponsored, said Elizabeth, a former member. “Mike was the one who determined how we lived our lives and instituted rules,” said another former member. There were daily check-ins with sponsors, who offered instructions on everything from who to date, where to work, whether to attend a family gathering, what kind of car to buy and what diet to follow. Personal information about how one may have wronged another person – referred to as a “fearless moral inventory” – would be shared with sponsors, and sometimes make its way to Quinones, where it could be used in a coercive way, former members allege. Dr Ellen Dye, a clinical psychologist based in Rockville, Maryland, who was quoted in the 2007 articles, said she had heard rumors about Midtown for years, including that it was cultlike. Then one of her patients got clean and joined the group. “She had a very scripted life that I’d never heard of before at AA. Everyone was telling her what she could and could not do. They even picked a boyfriend for her and were controlling her life,” Dye recalled. When Dye tried to point out that what was happening was not normal, her patient insisted that it was and left therapy. Ultimately, the patient came back to her and told Dye she believed Midtown was a sexually exploitative cult. She asked Dye to participate in the Newsweek article to get the word out. Dye recalled her patient telling her that Quinones had said “you won’t be able to drink if my dick is in your mouth”. Lacie W, a former member of Midtown, said she could also remember men making that “joke”. “It was said in front of young women and teenagers. In my opinion, it was said in the form of a joke, but also to pave the way for that to happen. Like as if to say, if that happens, it’s not a big deal. It is part of the process,” Lacie W said. Dye said she was not an expert in defining a cult, but that her patient had begun to act like someone who was under coercive control, similarly to a person who is in an abusive relationship. When a person in such a situation is confronted, she said, they will often quote the person who is controlling them to defend their actions, instead of expressing their own opinions. Tammy S said she joined Midtown in 1996, when she was 28 and Quinones was in his early 50s. She recalled how 72 hours after they met, he informed her they would be having sex. She began to date him and lived with him for two years. “I was older so it gave him some reprieve from the reputation that he only dated teenagers,” Tammy S said, though she points out he once told her he believed she had the mentality of a 13-year-old. She said she remembers overhearing conversations among older men about how it was important to have sex with teenagers in Maryland, where the age of consent was 16, and not in Virginia, where it was 18. When she brought it up she was told it was not her business to be the “arbiter of any one else’s sex conduct”. “That’s the way it went. You were shunned if you questioned things,” she said. She and Quinones eventually broke up. Shortly before his death, Quinones admitted to Tammy S that he had sexual relations with a 15-year-old. But he blamed the teenage girl for coming on to him. Mandi Pagliarini, now 44, was a member of Midtown from age 15 to 22, and now posts about her experience of what she calls “child trafficking and child violation” on Instagram. In one post, Pagliarini described how, like other young people she met, she never really needed a 12-step program. When her parents discovered she was smoking pot, she was sent to an adolescent treatment facility – a hospital – which in turn instructed her to attend “90 meetings in 90 days” as part of her discharge instructions. The hospital staff referred her to Midtown, which was known for being a young people’s group. There were cute high school and college-aged boys there, and Pagliarini quickly adopted an entire social life around the group. Amid the sorority-like fun, she said, were acts of labor, and daily self-analysis and confession to a sponsor. There were “verbal lashings”, strict diets for girls, and a “constant cycle” of fear and shame – followed often by love bombing, a form of manipulation in which someone is inundated with affection. Eventually, Pagliarini said, she began to be “nudged” toward older men, initially those in their late 20s and 30s. And then even older men. “We were structured like a pyramid, with the old-timers at the top, holding the power. The higher up the pyramid I was nudged, the more privileges and less labor I had to perform,” she said in one Instagram post. She was eventually sent to “Mike”. “The consequence of resistance outweighed enduring the act,” she wrote in a post on Instagram. Pagliarini and other sources have described how Quinones appeared to be relatively wealthy. She has said she realized later that men were giving him money, including the proceeds of any events. Several sources said Quinones would be gifted large items, including a luxury car and vacations. There was a kind of tithing system, in which members paid his rent and took him out to eat, former members allege. Adam Johnson was just 13 when he joined Midtown in 2005 and stayed for five years. During his most active years, he was attending a meeting every day – seven days a week – and believes one of the most troubling aspects of the group was the way members were expected not only to provide their sponsors with an “inventory” of the bad things they had done, including resentments, but also a “sexual inventory”. At the time, he trusted his sponsor. But now he realized the act of sharing such information was “a threat that had power over me”. Unlike a therapist, sponsors were not bound by secrecy. Johnson said it was considered completely normal for 15-year-old girls to be “dating” 20- or 21-year-old men, though he was not personally aware of instances of sexual trafficking of girls to even older men. Johnson said it was ingrained in people that there were addicts and there were “normal” people, and that this belief helped older members justify to others and themselves that a 15-year-old girl had more in common with a fellow addict who was in his 20s than a boy her age. Claire Perna joined Midtown and got sober when she was 16, in 2001, and remembers how when she first met Quinones, he seemed older than her parents. He was like a grandfather figure, she said. Given the age difference, she said in her own mind she never saw him as a threat. He first came on to her when she was a few months sober. He invited her to his house and she recalled how they walked into his bedroom and lay on his bed together. She was uncomfortable and got out of the situation without having sex with him. But when she told her sponsor what happened, and that it had been weird, she remembers seeing a look of disappointment and disapproval on her sponsor’s face. “Quinones really groomed me. After the first time he tried to have sex with me, he altered his approach and focused on the flattery, extra attention, how we were alike and other people wouldn’t really understand us,” she said. By the time she turned 17, Perna said she was regularly having sex with Quinones, as well as other much older men in the group. So was a friend of hers who was even younger than she was. “I think that that group was about men … Women were just objects for entertainment,” she said. Her recollection of Carr was as someone who was jovial, laughing at jokes with friends, and a little condescending. He seemed like a “cool college kid”, she said. Perna said she believed a number of adult members were aware of her relationship with Quinones, but that she did not believe Carr knew. “When I had three years sober, something cracked. I just couldn’t take it any more,” she said. She moved back with her parents. Perna only realized how completely Midtown deviated from normal AA when she started attending regular AA meetings. “I am grateful for my life today but I feel very sad for the person I was, that I spent so much of my life in that group, where I was gaslit to think that things that are so fucked-up were acceptable and normal,” she said. The publication of the Newsweek and Washington Post articles in 2007 had an immediate effect: the church on 22nd and P Street, where the group had its usual big Sunday meeting, kicked Midtown out, sources said. Quinones had been ill and some of his power had transferred to his lieutenants before his death that year. Over time, there was a slow exodus from the group, Lydia and other sources said, as people began to “grow up and get older”. “Once you got to your 30s and 40s, people began to think, ‘What the hell am I doing here?’” she said. An AA group called Midtown still exists today, and meets in suburban Maryland, on the outskirts of Washington. Sources who spoke to the Guardian say it is not the group it once was and there are no allegations that Midtown today – nearly two decades after Quinones’ death from cancer – is like a cult. *** Carr, who was appointed as chair of the FCC by Trump, wields his power in unprecedented ways, particularly against the president’s perceived enemies. Last year Jimmy Kimmel was temporarily taken off the air shortly after the FCC chair blasted the late-night host for comments he made following the murder of Charlie Kirk. Carr later defended his comments, saying local affiliates were “obligated” to scrutinize entertainment content that “does not serve the public interest”. When Trump recently criticized NBC journalist Kristen Welker, Carr suggested the FCC was “weighing options”, and issued a warning to broadcasters not to air “fake polls” that could suppress voters heading into midterm elections. Carr – who has been photographed wearing a golden lapel pin of Trump’s head – has defended his rhetoric, saying he is simply trying to force broadcasters to “operate in the public interest, not some sort of narrow, partisan interest”. Victor Pickard, a media professor at the Annenberg School for Communication at the University of Pennsylvania, said Carr had jettisoned his principles to serve “one man” in the White House and does not even pretend to be independent. “There was never a perfect FCC that exhibited zero partisanship,” he said. But as a scholar, he noted that “never in history” has there been such an “extreme capture” of the regulator as there is today. “Nothing is remotely similar,” he said. “He seems to wake up every day trying to figure out how he can serve Donald Trump,” Pickard added. In the opening paragraphs of a profile of Carr published by Bloomberg Businessweek in March, it noted how Carr was largely “unnotable and unnoticed” when he was an undergraduate student at Georgetown University. Carr has emerged as such a powerful enforcer in Trump’s Washington – having sparred publicly with Kimmel and Stephen Colbert – that alumni from the elite Jesuit college later scoured their yearbook to see if it was true that this young man whom they could not remember had graduated with them in 2001. The yearbook contained just a single mention of his name among a “slightly sorrowful list of unpictured students”, the article noted. Carr’s involvement in Midtown was not included in this or any other published profile. But two biographical facts contained in the Businessweek article are consistent with Carr’s Midtown affiliation. First, that the boy who had grown up in McLean, Virginia – a suburban, wealthy and relatively conservative enclave, famously close to CIA headquarters – had stayed close to home during his college years: one year at James Madison University in Virginia, then transferring to Georgetown, followed by law school at the Catholic University, in north-east Washington. It was understood inside Midtown, sources said, that members were not to stray too far from DC. Second, the profile noted that Carr had lived in a “group house” in Silver Spring, Maryland, “with a group of home-town buddies”. He was living with other members of Midtown. There was an “expectation” that Midtown members would live exclusively with other Midtown members, former members say. The stated intention was to support people’s sobriety, but one source said it also made it more difficult to leave the group. Carr lived for about two years in the Silver Spring home with three other Midtown members, public records indicate. One roommate who was interviewed by the Guardian said Carr was one of his best friends at the time. An internal 2002 Midtown phone directory indicates that Carr later moved to a home in Vienna, Virginia. Three other Midtown members shared the address, including Francisco Convit, a Venezuelan who was studying at university at the time. The Department of Justice now considers Convit to be a fugitive following his indictment for money laundering in 2018. He is a cousin of Alejandro Betancourt, a Venezuelan tycoon who is described as Trump’s partner in his bid to control Venezuelan oil resources. Adam Kaufmann, a lawyer who represented Convit, did not provide a comment to the Guardian about Convit’s apparent membership in Midtown or his living arrangements at the time. Asked about his living arrangements during those years, a spokesperson for Carr at the FCC denied he lived in a “Midtown group home”. The spokesperson did not respond to specific questions about Carr’s roommates during that period, who sources say were members of the group. The spokesperson did not respond to questions about Convit. The Guardian has heard two recordings of Carr when he was still in Midtown. In one, he described his upbringing, how he had gotten drunk about 10 times before he joined Midtown, and how someone had said – seemingly as a joke – that he could get a date to the prom if he joined AA. He also spoke of getting sober, of his need for other people’s approval and of the importance sobriety had played in his household. Midtown was described as “a lot more than a meeting to me”. Carr was described by one former member as a “victim of Midtown”, who was a young kid who got trapped, they said. “He was never involved in anything shady, and was actually the reverse, quite a stand-up guy. I was the sponsor to all the young girls and know all the predators well. Brendan was never among them,” the person said. She also said Carr “would never” have instructed people he sponsored to sleep with another person, although he “was sponsored by people who would”. A former member said he believed it was evident at the time to people inside Midtown that inappropriate things were happening. “He knew the deal and he hung around there … I did the same thing. But I should not be the chair of the FCC, either,” the former member said. A spokesperson for Carr has denied he had any knowledge of inappropriate conduct occurring at Midtown. Another person who spoke to the Guardian about her experience with Carr but did not want to be identified speaking about him said Midtown had “hijacked the name AA to bring people in”, and was full of kids from prominent and well-to-do families. Carr’s own father was a successful lawyer who once worked for Richard Nixon. “A lot of kids were from prep schools, and you got busted drinking or with drugs and you were sent to Midtown to ‘learn a lesson’ and just got trapped,” the woman, who dated Carr, said. While the woman was deeply critical of Midtown, she expressed warmth toward Carr. “Mike [Quinones] liked women who were bone thin. We were all eating next to nothing and Brendan would sneak me fries because he cared about me and knew I was hungry. That sounds like a stupid and small thing, but he could have been severely punished for that,” she said. A spokesperson for Carr at the FCC did not respond to questions about this alleged incident. The woman continued: “Brendan got gobbled up like everyone else. Here is the thing. Mike Quinones was in his 50s and liked to sleep with young girls. And there were some older men at the top, his lieutenants. But you are not going to get a 15-year-old like me to hang out [if there are not young men there]. You needed younger guys to serve as bait,” she said. The woman said one of her most distinct memories of Carr was coming home and seeing him sitting at the kitchen table and sobbing, because he had “bombed” his LSAT, the standardized test students take before they apply to law school. “His dad had a whole plan for his life and he wanted so badly to please him and was beside himself. And I was like, ‘You are going to take them again and you’re going to be fine.’ And he eventually went on, obviously, and did all that,” she said, adding: “He is one of the most tender souls and so desperate to please, and desperate to have a place to belong.” “He was such a fragile guy,” she said. A spokesperson for Carr at the FCC did not respond to questions about this alleged incident. The woman who dated Carr – who says she is apolitical – shared a message she sent Carr over Facebook, around the time when his first conflict with Kimmel was in the news. “Whether you’ve taken much time to consider it or not, I think you can admit the environment we grew up in was very unhealthy. And though you could probably surmise, it was way worse for the girls,” she wrote, pointing to the brutality of “forced ‘relationships’, restrictive diets, and psychological beatings”. She thanked Carr for being a “consistent, safe respite” and said she believed that both she and Carr had been among the most “fervent defenders” of Midtown “when called to do so” because they were the “hungriest” for belonging. She closed the letter with a plea: “You are fortified in yourself as a man – a man who has a family of his own now. You do not need the approval, or validation of anyone outside of you. You have your own table now, you don’t need to earn a seat at anyone else’s. He is Mike, Brendan. And I know you know that.” It was a reference to Trump. He did not reply to the letter, though she believes he read it.

webTitle: In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed’s candidacy has split the Jewish community

fields.headline: In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed’s candidacy has split the Jewish community
fields.trailText: The Democratic Senate nominee’s views on Israel and comments after a synagogue attack prompted a public debate among Jewish voters
fields.bodyText: When Jess Newman heard that Temple Israel in Detroit was attacked last March, her first thoughts went to her extended family. “I grew up going to services there,” she said. “The attack was awful. My Jewish identity is very important to me.” On 12 March, Ayman Ghazali, a naturalized US citizen from Lebanon, drove his truck into the Temple Israel, causing a fire and injuring a security guard. But even amid her anxiety for her family, Newman was startled by the response from some community members. “The reaction to it from people close to it that I know in my family is: ‘We need AK-47s under our beds,’” she recalled. Today Newman, a political organizer who sits on the Ferndale school board, spends about 10 hours a week volunteering for the campaign of Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel who is the Democratic party’s candidate to become US senator for Michigan in November’s midterm elections. “There is a problem with antisemitism,” she says. “I think it is made all that much harder to deal with when you can’t have a sensible conversation about why violence is happening … you cannot divorce violence invited upon people from violence being done around the world.” Newman’s experiences reflect the broader disagreements facing Michigan’s diverse Jewish communities this year. An estimated 130,000 Jewish Americans live in Michigan, where a 2021 study reported that 61% identified with or leaned Democrat and that Jewish adults are less likely to identify or lean Republican (31%) than all Michigan adults (42%). El-Sayed won the Democratic party’s Senate primary last month by just 15,000 votes. In a battleground state, El-Sayed’s unapologetically progressive campaign focuses on affordability rather than conflict in the Middle East, which has drawn ire from Republicans. But his positions on Israel-Palestine, including calling for an end to offensive and defensive military aid from the US, have become the focus of an active campaign to urge Jewish Michiganders to vote for his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers – as well as a counter-effort on El-Sayed’s behalf. *** Just six miles north-west of Newman’s progressive Ferndale neighborhood, Oak Park is the heartbeat of Michigan’s Orthodox Jewish community, home to Jewish retirement homes, synagogues and kosher bakeries. On the eve of the recent Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was a steady stream of customers buying bread and sweet treats from kosher stores as children furiously cycled from the stores to a nearby synagogue. It was here, last April, that antisemitic graffiti was sprayed on the outside a synagogue. “In the Jewish community, I think we have an awareness that it’s not if something is going to happen, it’s when something is going to happen. This isn’t the first incident we’ve had here,” Rabbi Robert Gamer of the Congregation Beth Shalom told CBS Detroit in April. El-Sayid was criticized for comments he made in March about the Temple Israel attack, saying, in part, that “hurt people hurt people”, referring to the Temple Israel attacker. An FBI investigation concluded that the attacker was inspired by Hezbollah. Ghazali’s two brothers, a niece and a nephew, had been killed in an Israeli airstrike in southern Lebanon days before. The Democratic candidate has also drawn criticism for links to Hasan Piker, the leftwing streamer who has become a target for attacks from Republicans and centrist Democrats. In the Democratic primary, El-Sayed lost Oak Park’s Oakland county to Haley Stevens by nearly 20,000 votes – a number larger than his final winning margin. El-Sayed later apologized for those comments, saying that he had jumped too quickly to provide “context” for the attack, “but it wasn’t the time for context”. Still, El-Sayed’s message has particularly resonated with young Jewish Michiganders angered by the variety of challenges facing working people, and aligned with his positions on Israel. Since his primary win, he has made a concerted effort to meet with Jewish leaders, including the Michigan Democratic Jewish caucus, which has not yet endorsed him. Several campaign initiatives reflect divisions among Jewish communities. An open letter supporting El Sayed, signed by Michigan Jews for Democracy, has about 1,000 signatures. Other rabbis and Jewish leaders have formed the Nonnegotiable Michigan campaign, a petition that demands, among other things, that candidates for office support “Jewish sovereignty in Israel”. (El-Sayed has said he supports “equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination” for both Israeli and Palestinians, through whatever political system both peoples choose.) A third initiative is openly calling for Jewish Democrats and independents to back Rogers, claiming: “All of us have felt threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed.” In June, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), a pro-Palestine organization that represents about 750,000 members and supporters nationwide, endorsed El-Sayed in a first for the organization, helping him defeat Stevens, who received tens of millions of dollars from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), the pro-Israel Super Pac. Others joined after the primary results were settled. “After the primary, some of the members of our [T’chiyah] congregation who voted for Stevens started showing up to the Jews for Abdul meetings because they were just like: ‘We don’t totally align with him on [Israel], but we are very clear that the alternative is really bad,’” says Jackson Koeppel, a 33-year-old Detroit-based volunteer with Jews for Abdul, a group critical of Israel, citing El-Sayed’s platform on universal healthcare and getting money out of politics. Last month, Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, asked Aipac not to publicly spend advertising money on his own behalf, acknowledging a growing concern Michigan voters have with the powerful pro-Israel lobbying organization. Polls have put El-Sayed and Rogers in a dead heat. For Josh Whinston, a rabbi at Temple Beth Emeth in Ann Arbor, a reform congregation, it was comments El-Sayed made the morning after his primary win last month that prompted significant concern. “When I hear Dr El-Sayed, the morning after the primary, talk about Israel as bloodthirsty and then in the evening tell me that he cared about my security, that really created such a dissonance in my head,” said Whinston, who has joined the “Nonnegotiable” initiative. He said he viewed the term “bloodthirsty” as playing into an antisemitic trope. At the same time, Whinston, who has met El-Sayed in a one-on-one meeting, says his door is not closed to the idea of voting for the Democrat. “He is an inspiring leader I think he has the potential to do amazing things in our country,” he says. “He is moving in the right direction; he has not moved far enough.” Meanwhile, Republicans and rightwing media have seized on his platform. Last month, vice-president JD Vance spoke personally with a rabbi and a security guard from Temple Israel, who also attended a rally Vance held in nearby Sterling Heights in which the vice-president claimed El-Sayed is “very, very evil”. (Temple Israel declined an interview request from the Guardian.) El-Sayed’s campaign also faces a formidable challenge in the shape of big sums of out-of-state campaign spending. “In Detroit, we have a lot of work to do in terms of getting people excited,” says Newman. Elon Musk has already spent $1m in Michigan on online ads targeting El-Sayed. For his part, Newman, who went on a birthright trip to Israel when she was 18, says the contrast between El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, and Rogers, who with his wife has a net worth of between $7m and $14m, is clear. “He’s principled; he believes in and has actually done work to build better conditions for people in the [Michigan] health departments,” she says. “He’s running a campaign that I can respect; he’s not taking any corporate money, which is a huge piece of this.” • This article was amended on 23 September 2026 to clarify that Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic party’s candidate to represent Michigan in the US Senate in the midterm elections, rather than a candidate for the Michigan senate.

webTitle: AI is generating a new wave of US populism. It could be a tipping point | Robert Reich

fields.headline: AI is generating a new wave of economic populism. It could be a tipping point
fields.trailText: It’s becoming obvious to many Americans that corporations have been raking it in while workers take it on the chin
fields.bodyText: Last week, the unlikely duo of Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon spoke before a Washington group demanding a stop to AI and its datacenters. Notably, both lambasted the corporate oligarchs behind AI. The most potent force in US politics is anti-establishment fury at a system seen as rigged against average working people. AI has become exhibit A. Until recently, both parties largely avoided criticizing the wealthy corporate elites that funded their campaigns. In politics as in nature, one does not bite the hands that feed. Trump Republicans have instead aimed populist fury at immigrants, LGBTQ+ people, Black and Latino people, “communists”, Muslims, so-called “woke” leaders, “coastal elites”, “childless cat ladies” and other scapegoats. Democrats – with the exceptions of Sanders, AOC and a few others – have also avoided criticizing wealthy corporate elites, aiming their populist fury at Trump. This may be changing. It’s becoming obvious to much of the US that giant corporations have been raking it in while workers have been taking it on the chin. As of mid-2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the percentage of the total economy going to workers as wages had fallen to a record low of 52.9% (down from above 65% when tracking began in 1947) – leaving the rest to investors, business owners, and corporate profits. AI is on the way to causing far more inequality – generating billions for its backers while reducing the number of jobs and real wages. Trump and his regime, meanwhile, have exposed the greed, venality, cupidity and corruption of the US’s wealthy corporate elites by allowing them to do anything they wish – including create energy-guzzling, water-depleting AI datacenters – as long as they kiss his assets by funding his Pac, paying for his ballroom and singing his praises. Trump has thereby revealed the truth about corporate America that for years had been hidden behind corporate PR about “corporate social responsibility”, corporate charity and “trickle-down” economics: the captains of corporate America are willing to throw average working Americans under the bus to make billions more. Corporate avarice under Trump has become so blatant and corporate America’s contempt for the needs of average Americans so flagrant that most Americans are now catching on. In a recent NBC poll, 54% of Americans agreed that “when it comes to politics and society, nothing really matters because powerful people will always do whatever they want.” AI may well be the final tipping point. Data centers are unpopular – about 70% of the public opposes them. And Americans harbor deep suspicions of AI. More than 60% believe AI could destroy humanity (this includes 60% of Trump supporters). Fears about AI are provoking larger concerns about wealthy corporate elites bribing politicians – not just to get generous subsidies for AI but also to reduce the corporate elite’s tax bills, kill off unions, slash social safety nets, deregulate Wall Street, attain no-bid government contracts, receive exclusive licenses, open tax loopholes, get tariff exemptions, use public lands, and become even bigger monopolies. Because of Trump, Americans are coming to view those wealthy corporate elites as more aligned with Republicans than with Democrats. According to last week’s Times-Sienna poll, when likely voters were asked which party the word “elitist” describes, a remarkable 43% said Republicans while 33% said Democrats. This is something of a return to how the US’s two major political parties used to be seen. Ninety years ago, Democrats were assumed to be on the side of working people against wealthy corporate elites. On the eve of his 1936 re-election, Franklin D Roosevelt told the American people they were fighting “business and financial monopoly, speculation, reckless banking, class antagonism, war profiteering … We now know that government by organized money is just as dangerous as government organized by the mob.” Will Democrats seize the moment and embrace the new AI-fueled economic populism? Or will they continue to succumb to the siren songs of big money? According to Politico, some Democratic political consultants are quietly urging candidates in the toughest battleground races to stay mum on AI “over fears that powerful and well-resourced pro-AI interest groups could spend money pummeling them in the final weeks of the midterms”. It’s not just the future of the Democratic party that’s at stake; it’s the future of America. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

webTitle: Trump’s bizarre social media blitz leaves world guessing ahead of UN address

fields.headline: Trump’s bizarre social media blitz leaves world guessing ahead of UN address
fields.trailText: President has been posting on Washington arch, AI and his ‘25 top achievements’ – the chances of an uplifting speech appear slim
fields.bodyText: The annual gathering of the United Nations general assembly has historically been a platform for US presidents to display their most serious face and a positive vision to the world. From Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower to John F Kennedy and Barack Obama, over eight decades US leaders have used the setting to expound on grand themes before a global audience at pivotal moments in international affairs. As world leaders and officials gather in New York for the yearly event, and Donald Trump prepares to address them on Tuesday, how he will contribute to this historic catalog of remarks is a matter of speculation. The US president has spent recent days blitzing social media on a variety of topics, from his planned triumphal arch in Washington to a bid to rebrand artificial intelligence, as he contends with an unpopular war and low approval ratings that threaten to drag down his party in November’s US midterm elections. His previous addresses to the assembly suggest that the chances of a non-divisive and uplifting message are low. Last year, Trump shocked the august gathering in his first appearance since returning to the White House the previous January by declaring to those present that their countries were “going to hell” while launching a full-frontal assault on the UN and the concept of open borders. In 2018, during his first presidency, Trump drew laughter from fellow leaders when he opened his address by claiming: “In less than two years, my administration has accomplished almost more than any other administration in the history of our country.” The previous year, he had attacked longstanding allies, singling out Germany for its energy policy, and declaring that the US “can no longer be taken advantage of, or enter into a one-sided deal where the United States gets nothing in return”. This time around, Trump’s recent social media activities hinted at an even more volatile than usual state of mind from a leader who can be erratic at the best of times. Arguably the most eye-catching was his declaration in an early Sunday morning post that he intended to turn his highly controversial planned arch in Washington DC into a military storage facility, claiming – without providing evidence – that the move was requested by the US military. There was a surfeit of others. A post headlined “His Hemisphere” and depicting Trump gazing at a map of the globe ominously hinted at an imperious tone he could strike, less than nine months after US forces seized the former Venezuelan leader, Nicolás Maduro, in his compound in Caracas and spirited him and his wife to New York. The Trump administration has since trumpeted a deal giving it control over a significant segment of Venezuelan oil reserves. In another post, Trump postures as the defender of AI – denouncing recent fears that its rapid development could presage the destruction of the human race. Instead, he painted it as the latest target of “many hoaxes, all generated by the radical left dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our country” and announced his plans for an “AI force”– headed by an “AI Czar” – in the image of the space force, established during his first presidency. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our country’s GDP,” he wrote. “We are leading China, and the rest of the world, and I intend to keep it that way.” There is every chance Trump returns to previous themes at the UN on Tuesday. In an echo of his 2018 speech, on Friday he posted a list of his “Top 25 Trump Achievements” since returning to office. Trump’s appearance before the general assembly will be his first since his fateful decision to launch, in tandem with Israel, a war against Iran in February. The conflict – despite his predictions that it would last a few days, and result in the collapse of Tehran’s Islamic regime – shows no signs of ending. The regime still stands. Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway that was a conduit to one-fifth of the world’s oil exports before hostilities began, has sent global energy prices soaring and stoked inflation in the US, challenging the prospects of Trump’s Republican party in November’s midterms. Polls show a majority of Americans oppose the war, which has further deflated his approval ratings. Further piquancy to Trump’s political dilemma is likely to be added by the presence of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, at the UN. While Trump has signaled a willingness to meet his Iranian counterpart, Pezeshkian – a relative pragmatist, under pressure from regime hardliners to stand firm and avoid compromise with an enemy still branded by Tehran as “the great Satan” – is thought unlikely to agree to such an encounter. The sting of being snubbed by an Iranian leadership he likes to depict as “dying to make a deal” could add further fuel to a fiery speech before the general assembly and witnessed by a global audience. Traditionally, US presidential speeches to the UN go through a long drafting process and are subject to reviews by the state department, the Pentagon and the intelligence community, as well as fevered last-minute rehearsals. That all may still hold true for this address. Yet equally likely is a no-holds-barred, scattergun diatribe, rehashing the themes of Trump’s recent social media output.

webTitle: Trump says he’ll probably lose lawsuit brought by news outlets he banned from White House, blaming judge appointed by ‘TRUMP’ – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump says he’ll probably lose lawsuit brought by news outlets he banned from White House, blaming judge appointed by ‘TRUMP’ – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: That concludes our coverage of the second Trump administration for today. Here are the latest developments: The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. Newsrooms including the New York Times and the Washington Post also decided to hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage on Monday until midnight as part of the collective effort. More here. The barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights. The parties are seeking a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban – and return access for the journalists – while the case plays out. More here. Trump is bracing for a loss in the lawsuit brought by the three media organizations, as he considers that the judge presiding over the case – his own appointee – previously ordered the White House to restore credentials for journalist Jim Acosta. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote on Truth Social. Trump said that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. More here. At a news conference following their closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion, Mamdani said he and Trump held a “wide-ranging” discussion, which touched on affordable housing and immigration. The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. More here. Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. More here. A long-running legal fight over Missouri’s congressional map took another turn Monday when a federal appeals panel ruled in favor of new districts backed by Donald Trump, even though the US supreme court has blocked those districts from being used in the November election, the AP reports. A three-judge panel of the eighth US circuit court of appeals said Missouri should use the new Republican-drawn US House districts in the November election, just as the state did in its August primary. To revert to its prior districts for the general election would violate the US constitution, the appeals judges said. However, the ruling has no immediate impact. That’s because the federal appellate panel delayed the effect of its order for a week to allow time for an appeal. The US supreme court already has twice sided against the Trump-backed map and had blocked enforcement of a lower court order favoring the map pending a potential appeal and eventual decision by the high court. Missouri is currently set to run its November election with the same congressional districts it used in 2024 and 2022, following prior decisions by both the Missouri supreme court and the US supreme court. Read the full story here: In a press conference held on Monday, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani was in disagreement with Donald Trump’s decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, and instead welcomed all members of the press at Gracie Mansion in New York. “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in – is everyone, no matter the opinion or the critique, that we engage,” Mamdani said. US Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff are asking California attorney general Rob Bonta to look into the claims of a whistleblower alleging the Department of Homeland Security is ordering officers to impersonate voters to access online voter data. According to the senators, officers in a unit of the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), an agency within the department, are being tasked with investigating 40 subjects per day. The whistleblower claims that officers were instructed to pull citizens’ personal data from federal databases and enter it into the state website to gain access. “The Trump Administration appears to be undertaking this rushed effort to find – or manufacture – evidence for its baseless election conspiracy theories of widespread voter fraud ahead of the 2026 midterm elections,” reads a letter by the senators. “Inaccurate claims of ‘unlawful voters’ and erroneous federal law enforcement records can result in serious consequences for Californians, including many naturalized citizens.” “The Trump Administration may also use these claims to further threaten state and local election officials in California and undermine or challenge the election results themselves,” the senators added in the letter. US Representative Ro Khanna said on Monday that the shooting of a Venezuelan man in Texas by a federal immigration officer “demands a full investigation”. “No one should be shot in the back and denied urgent medical care,” Khanna wrote in a post on social media. “The shooting of Venezuelan DoorDash driver Wilber Garcés Pérez by ICE in Austin demands a full investigation.” Khanna added: “Abolish ICE. Prosecute rogue agents.” Earlier today, Garcés Pérez pleaded for better medical care. “I haven’t received any medical attention. I’m in a lot of pain,” he said. My colleague Emiliano Tahui Gomez is reporting the latest details on the shooting: The US is planning to reopen a former cold war-era ⁠military base in southern Greenland and set up a military presence at an east coast base, Reuters reports. Sources told the wire that an agreement is expected to be signed by the US, Denmark and Greenland on Tuesday at the United Nations general assembly in New ‌York City. One of these military bases, Mestersvig, ⁠is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol. The other post is Narsarsuaq, where the population has dwindled to a few dozen people since the US closed its Bluie West One military base in the 1950s. The agreement follows the announcement of an Arctic security pact between the US and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, following pressure from Trump to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force. In his remarks today, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani said he shared “very strong opinions” on “how we can keep immigrant New Yorkers safe” during his meeting with Donald Trump, especially regarding temporary protected status (TPS) for immigrants in the United States. Mamdani said he told the US president “how important immigrant New Yorkers, especially Haitian New Yorkers, are not only to the fabric of our city, but also to our city’s economy, to so many of the industries that build our city, and the stability that is in the president’s hands”. In June, the US supreme court ruled in favor of the Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS from hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians. Zohran Mamdani was asked whether he challenged Donald Trump on the banning of CNN, MS Now, and Politico from White House grounds. “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in,” Mamdani said at Gracie Mansion in New York City. “It’s interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn’t very worried about that,” Trump said. In response to a question about whether the ban was put in place as a distraction from the war in Iran and high gas prices, Trump said: “I’m not.” “I’m only doing it because I think the press also has an obligation,” Trump said. “I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair. And if they’re fake news, I really think I have an obligation not to allow them into another very special house. This is a special house, Gracie Mansion. Well, the White House is the most special of all houses.” New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani and President Donald Trump spoke ahead of the UN General Assembly this week following a closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion on Monday. “One of the focuses of the conversation the president and I have been having is about the possibility of building more housing here in New York City,” Mamdani said. “We’ve spoken about Sunnyside Yard,” he added, referring to the 180-acre railyard in Queens, “and it’s a real pleasure that just today we’ve agreed to set up a new level of that conversation between our housing and operations team at City Hall and the White House team.” “I can tell you that Sunnyside’s a big job,” Trump said. “I’ve been watching that for 35 years. Everybody’s wanted to do something with Sunnyside Yards.” “You’re going to need a lot of federal approvals and probably some federal money to do it. But it’s always been a great location,” Trump added. The New York Times said it would hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage on Monday until midnight, joining a collective effort with photographers in other newsrooms in support of the media organizations that were banned from the White House. “The New York Times will not publish or distribute any images taken as part of the White House still photography pool today, in conjunction with the other members of that pool and in a show of support for the news organizations being unfairly targeted by the president’s barring of journalists from the White House,” said Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesperson for the news outlet, in a statement. “We remain committed to covering the president’s travel to New York City today,” Stadtlander added. “Americans deserve a free and independent media covering their government without intimidation, as well as comprehensive coverage of newsworthy events.” Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, the Venezuelan man who was shot by an ICE officer in Austin, spoke over the phone at a news conference, offering further details on his condition. The 28-year-old was taken to a hospital in Austin, Texas, in serious but stable condition before being taken into custody. The Associated Press reports that, speaking by phone during a news conference, Garcés Pérez said doctors didn’t remove the bullet because it’s near his spine. He said ICE pressed for him to be released quickly from the hospital so officers could move him to a detention center. He said he had received no pain medication or treatment there, and had slept on the floor before eventually being given a “pill” by a nurse on Monday. “I am not doing well due to the gunshot wound, and I have not received the medical attention that I require,” Perez said, speaking in Spanish over the phone as his wife translated during the news conference. Donald Trump is bracing for a loss in the lawsuit brought by three media organizations, as he considers that the judge presiding over the case – his own appointee – previously ordered the White House to restore credentials for journalist Jim Acosta. “They have drawn a great Judge, for them, a man who ruled in favor of Jim Acosta, who now seems to have disappeared from the Planet,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, referring to a lawsuit filed by CNN in 2018. “The Judge’s name is Tim Kelly, and he was, sadly, appointed by ‘TRUMP.’ In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.” President Donald Trump has arrived at Gracie Mansion to meet with New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, per CNN. In a post on Truth Social, Trump called the official residence of New York City’s mayors “one of my favorite places in the World.” “It will be interesting to see how it looks now, invited by Mayor Mamdani,” Trump wrote. “Look forward to it. MAKE NEW YORK CITY GREAT AGAIN!” It appears the media boycott of President Trump in response to his banning of several news outlets from the White House has expanded from video coverage to include still images. On Monday afternoon, The Washington Post said in a statement posted to social media that it would not publish any photos of Trump until midnight. “The Washington Post will not publish any photographs of today’s presidential events – including Trump’s departure from the White House and his events at the United Nations in New York – until midnight Eastern Time, joining a collective effort with photographers in other newsrooms covering the White House in a show of support of the banned outlets.” It was unclear which other outlets, if any, had joined the Post’s roughly 8-hour moratorium on sharing images of the president. Three news outlets sued after Trump blocked them from the White House. If you missed it, Trump on Friday announced a surprise decision to ban Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House, citing unfavorable coverage of his administration. On Monday, the three outlets, as anticipated, filed a lawsuit to restore their access. The other White House TV pool members paused coverage of Trump in solidarity. The pool, for the uninitiated, is a rotation of five major networks (ABC, NBC, CBS, Fox News, and the recently axed CNN) who take turns following the president day-to-day and sharing their collected footage with other outlets. After Trump’s decision to nix CNN, the other four outlets agreed to cease covering the president as per usual, so far leaving Trump bereft of his usual tag-along camera crew. Some key Republicans are pressing their president hard on war-inflated diesel prices. As the war in Iran continues to jack up the price of diesel — the fuel that runs America’s semi trucks, tractors, and heavy machinery — some influential Republicans are coming out publicly to pressure the president to take more drastic action. Republican senator Chuck Grassley called for an embargo on diesel exports. And Republican congresswoman and Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson called for measures to tamp prices and bring an “immediate” end to the war in Iran. Trump is beginning a busy week of diplomacy. Trump is heading to New York to attend the United Nations’ annual convening of world leaders. While there, he’s expected to meet with a number of key heads of state, including the US-backed interim president of Venezuela, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and possibly the leaders of Iran. But first, Trump will be meeting with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a political opposite with whom he’s so far maintained a strange rapport. An ICE agent shot a DoorDash driver in Austin, Texas, on Sunday. The shooting — just the latest in a string of shootings by ICE agents enforcing the Trump administration’s deportation crackdown — prompted protests in the Texas capital. Donald Trump is expected to press Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week during United Nations high-level week, as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran, as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine. Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, launching its largest reported strike yet on the Moscow region in a barrage that struck a major Moscow oil refinery and killed three people. On Monday, Trump said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage that he said was being exacerbated by the war in Ukraine. “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Monday morning. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission.” “This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” Trump said. “The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!” Trump had earlier blamed Kyiv for the escalating energy war even as Russia has decimated Ukraine’s economy and launched night barrages of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities. Zelenskyy on Monday said negotiations were continuing and that that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps”. “Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” he said in a statement. “Solutions are possible.” The two leaders are expected to meet on Tuesday during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations general assembly. Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov will also be in Washington this week, and is expected to meet with secretary of state Marco Rubio. During a trip to Ireland last week, Trump directly addressed Zelenskyy, saying he has to do “one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”. “Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage,” he said. Trump spoke with Zelenskyy on Sunday in a phone call that one senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times was about “diesel, diesel, diesel”. Average diesel prices in the United States hit a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, up from $3.19 per gallon this time last year before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran and Tehran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz to most international trade. The rise in prices is seen as a liability for Trump’s Republican party in the US midterm elections, which will take place in November. Trump is expected to deliver a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday morning, and is expected to meet with major energy producers including the Gulf Cooperation Council and Venezuela’s recently installed leader Delcy Rodriguez. In a preview, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, said Trump would speak about how he has “confronted complex problems head-on around the world. Many of the peace deals that he has driven to conclusion, or is in the process of driving to conclusion.” Trump last week prematurely announced an energy ceasefire under which Ukraine had agreed not to hit Russian energy targets and that “Russia has agreed to do likewise!” The deal had not been agreed, however, and Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure have continued. After a ribbon cutting ceremony not covered by the standard White House TV press pool, Trump boarded Marine One, en route to New York City for a planned meeting with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and, later, French President Emmanuel Macron. The White House streamed video of Trump’s remarks. However, the audio was too distorted to make out what he said. Ashley Hinson, a Republican member of the House of Representatives campaigning for a valuable Senate seat in Iowa, publicly called for an end to the war with Iran in a social media post on Monday. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.” After listing some potential policy measures to mitigate the costs of diesel fuel, she added: “These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.” While Hinson didn’t name Trump outright, her comments diverge from the oft-repeated stance of a president who has said the high prices are a worthwhile setback to bring Iran’s leadership to heel. Hinson, once a steady ally of Trump, has drifted further from the president in recent weeks. When JD Vance, a key surrogate for Trump on the 2026 campaign trail, headlined a rally in her state last week, Hinson was notably absent. Her comment also comes as Republicans worry that the unpopular conflict will hamstring the party in the midterm elections and help secure control of one or both chambers of Congress for the Democrats. JD Vance defended Trump’s ban of three news outlets from the White House while speaking to reporters en route to a campaign event in North Carolina. “He’s not banning media outlets,” Vance said on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews. (Trump, in his social media post announcing the move, referred to his actions as a ban.) Vance continued: “What he’s doing is saying we’re not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda.” He criticized the outlets for coverage that he said was overly negative of the Trump administration. “That’s not representative of the American people. It’s not representative of public opinion. So if you’re going to engage in what is effectively far left propaganda, why would a Republican White House give you special access?” But, he said, Trump’s actions didn’t violate the outlets’ rights, because “they can still report on the Trump White House, they can still get the public reports” and “they can still, of course, talk to people in the administration and outside the administration”. “It’s about basic fairness. They can still report. They still have access to free speech. They’re just not going to get an office in the White House anymore. And I think it’s totally appropriate, unless, of course, they start to behave like real news organizations.” Donald Trump is facing growing calls, including from within his own party, to boost support for US farmers as his administration faces mounting anger over its treatment of the agricultural sector. Republican senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa called on the US president to place an embargo on diesel exports this weekend and help farmers grapple with high prices. Grassley, who is largely aligned with Trump, suggested the embargo in multiple social media posts, calling on the president to issue a 1970s-style embargo on diesel and agricultural products to help farmers. “If our [government] can embargo chips to China it can embargo diesel to help American farmers & truckers,” Grassley wrote on Sunday. “We need our family farmers who feed&fuel the world [to be] on the strongest footing possible no matter what’s happening across the globe.” For months, farmers – traditionally a reliable Republican voting base – have been angry with the Trump administration because they believe some of its policies adversely affect them. That includes tariffs, which have driven up the cost of fertilizer, machine parts, seed and more; increasing beef imports to lower prices for Americans, which undermines domestic producers; and the Iran war, which has made it more expensive for farmers to operate machinery and transport products. The national average cost of diesel was $6.51 as of Sunday, according to AAA. In Iowa, it was slightly lower at $6.31 – still nearly $3 more than the cost one year ago. Gas prices are not the only rising cost Americans are facing as a result of the Iran war. Groceries have also become more expensive, and the Trump administration has sought to lower some of those prices, particularly beef, by allowing 300,000 metric tons of overseas beef trimmings to enter the US at a reduced tariff rate. But domestic farmers in the US, who are already struggling with smaller herds, say the decision will increase competition and make it more difficult to sell their own. “It takes something big to change long-established voting patterns, but I think there’s a possibility that the Trump administration has done things that are big enough and bad enough from the standpoint of rural America to make some of the voters who shifted a decade ago reconsider their choice,” William Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told the Washington Sun. South America correspondent A special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that the United States attacks on boats allegedly carrying drugs in the Pacific and Caribbean “constituted crimes against humanity”. The boat strikes, carried out since September 2025 on the stated grounds of stopping drugs being trafficked by sea to the US, have killed more than 230 people. The latest, on Saturday, killed four people in the Caribbean. The UN itself, along with several human rights organisations, lawyers and international law experts, had already described the bombings as “extrajudicial killings”, but special rapporteur Ben Saul went further. In a briefing note posted by Saul on social media on Sunday night and first reported by the BBC, Saul wrote that, in addition to “serial extrajudicial killings”, the attacks were “in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law”. He added: “There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law.” The report cites 68 US attacks that killed 223 people. It is unclear how recently the figures were updated – tallies by organisations such as the Washington Office on Latin America put the death toll at 234 people in 66 attacks. US Southern Command, which has coordinated the attacks, posted on Saturday, alongside a grainy video, that it had “executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists”. As has become standard in announcements of such attacks, the US did not identify the victims or provide any details about the alleged intelligence that supposedly confirmed their involvement in drug trafficking. Saul’s report rejects the claim made by Donald Trump before Congress that the strikes amounted to “self-defence” against “designated terrorist organizations”. The special rapporteur wrote that the crews were not “militarily armed and possessed the intent and capacity to launch military attacks” against the US. “Even assuming that the vessels and crew attacked were members of the criminal groups listed as terrorist, such organizations have not mounted any ‘armed attack’ on the United States so as to trigger a right of self-defence,” he added. The US Department of State has not yet responded to a request for comment. Here’s our full report: Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Colorado Republican congresswoman, is the subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet. She said the allegations are untrue, and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. Boebert’s denials came through a formal statement from her office, which said “the congresswoman rejects the claims as utterly false”, and a verbose video rant on social media in which she accused the person who filed the document as a “sloppy, desperate, obsessive hack”, and journalists who reported the story as falling victim to a “scam”. According to the complaint, filed last week by David Wheeler, an independent journalist, activist, and founder of the American Muckrakers political action committee, Boebert committed at least seven violations of House ethics rules. Among the most prominent allegations are that Boebert conducted a four-year “romantic and sexual relationship” with a senior female staffer, named as Clarice Navarro Ratzlaff, then paid her $200,000 when Ratzlaff broke off the affair and threatened to file an ethics complaint of her own. Consent, the rules state, is not a defense. Boebert frequently promotes her own Christian values and has previously been publicly critical of same-sex relationships. Pritzker told CBS Mornings that he began taking GLP-1s after receiving a diabetes diagnosis two years ago. Since then, he said he’s lost 80 pounds.
